text: You have num courses courses, labeled zero to n minus one. You're given pairs a, b, meaning you must take course b before course a. Return any valid order to finish all courses. If it's impossible, return an empty array.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — a pair a, b is a dependency: b is a prerequisite of a, so b comes first. And the answer is an ordering where every course appears after all its prerequisites. Is that right?

When is it impossible? I think the only way it fails is if the dependencies form a cycle — course A needs B, B needs A. Then no valid order exists and I return an empty array. Is a cycle the only failure case?
Right. A cycle is the only reason it fails.
A couple more. Can the answer have more than one valid order? And are there any constraints on the input size?
Any valid order is accepted. Up to about two thousand courses and a few thousand pairs.

Let me run through the example. Say four courses, with pairs one-zero, two-zero, three-one, three-two. So zero unlocks one and two, and both one and two unlock three. A valid order is zero, one, two, three — or zero, two, one, three, since one and two don't depend on each other. That matches.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. This is a directed graph: each course is a node, each pair is a directed edge. Finishing all courses while respecting prerequisites is exactly a topological sort of that graph, and a topological order exists if and only if the graph has no cycle — which lines up with the one failure case. This problem reminds me of topological sorting, and there are two standard ways to build it. One is DFS post-order: finish a node only after all its descendants, then reverse. The other is Kahn's algorithm — a BFS that repeatedly removes nodes with no remaining prerequisites. Both run in O of V plus E. I'll code the DFS one and then show the Kahn variant.

Here's the plan for the DFS version. One: build an edge from b to a, so a prerequisite points to the course it unlocks. Two: DFS from every course with three states, and append a node to the order only after all its neighbors finish. Three: if any DFS finds a cycle, return empty; otherwise reverse the order. One thing worth flagging — the cycle check needs three states, not two. In a DAG a node can be reached again by a different path, and that's normal. Only re-entering a node still on the current recursion path is a real cycle; a plain visited flag would falsely flag the diamond's shared node. Why reverse? Post-order puts a node after its descendants; a topological order wants it before them. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?
DFS is good. Code it up.

Alright, let me code this up. I'll think out loud as I go. I build the edges from b to a, then run has cycle from every course and return empty on the first cycle; at the end I reverse the order. Inside has cycle, state one means I came back onto my path, state two means the node is already finished. Otherwise I mark it one, explore its neighbors, then mark it two and append it. One thing worth flagging — I set visit to two and push to the order after the loop over neighbors. That ordering is the whole point: the node is recorded only once every descendant is already recorded.

Let's dry-run the code on four courses, pairs one-zero, two-zero, three-one, three-two — so zero points to one and two, and both point to three. The row that matters is entering two and seeing three already in state two — that call returns right away, where a two-state flag would have called it a cycle. The finish order is three, one, two, zero, so reversed it's zero, two, one, three. Valid. Corner cases: one course and no pairs gives just zero. And the cycle zero-one, one-zero: from zero I reach one, whose edge leads back to zero, still in state one, so I return empty.
Good. You mentioned Kahn's algorithm earlier — can you show that version?

Sure. Instead of recursion, I track each node's in-degree — how many prerequisites it still has. I start a queue with every node at in-degree zero, and each time I pop one, I remove it by decrementing its neighbors; any neighbor that reaches zero joins the queue. The pop order is the answer. One thing worth flagging — here the cycle check is free. Nodes inside a cycle keep a positive in-degree forever, so they never enter the queue. If the order ends up shorter than num courses, some node was stuck in a cycle, and I return empty. Same O of V plus E, no recursion depth risk.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is O of V plus E for both — every node and edge is touched once. Space is O of V plus E for the adjacency list, plus O of V for the visit or in-degree arrays and the queue or recursion stack. Oh, one more thing — for very deep graphs the DFS recursion could risk a stack overflow, so in production I'd lean toward Kahn's iterative version. And if the problem wanted the lexicographically smallest order, I'd swap Kahn's plain queue for a min-heap.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You framed it as a topological sort and tied impossible precisely to a cycle. You caught that the DFS cycle check needs three states — and showed exactly where a two-state flag would break on the shared node. And you gave both algorithms with a clear reason to prefer the iterative one. Good work.
